questions.q: Who is the protagonist of "A Roadside Stand"? Answer in one sentence.
questions.a: The protagonist is the collective group of rural poor who run the roadside stand — the "pitiful kin" who wait for city money to alleviate their poverty. A wrong answer (e.g., "the poet" or "the city folk") reveals the student is confusing the speaker/observer with the central subject, or misidentifying antagonists as protagonists.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the poet describes the stand's signs as having "N turned wrong and S turned wrong". What does this detail reveal about the protagonist?
questions.a: The misspelled signs show the stand-owners' lack of formal education and resources, yet their effort to communicate ("artless paint") highlights dignity in struggle. A wrong answer that calls it "carelessness" or "humour" misses the sympathetic portrayal and the poem's critique of systemic neglect.

questions.q: Apply the concept of "trusting sorrow" (stanza 2) to analyse the protagonist's relationship with the city folk. Use two pieces of textual evidence.
questions.a: The phrase "trusting sorrow" captures the protagonists' naive hope that city dwellers will stop and buy ("ask for some city money to feel in hand"), contrasted with the reality that "thousand selfish cars" pass without inquiry. Evidence: (1) "And ask for some city money to feel in hand / To try if it will not make our being expand" — shows hope; (2) "Of all the thousand selfish cars that pass, / Just one to inquire what a farmer's prices are" — shows betrayal. A wrong answer that only quotes without linking hope to betrayal fails to analyse the dynamic.

questions.q: Analyse how the poet uses the image of "greedy good-doers, beneficent beasts of prey" (stanza 3) to deepen our understanding of the protagonist's vulnerability.
questions.a: The oxymoron "greedy good-doers" and metaphor "beneficent beasts of prey" expose how government schemes ("bought out and mercifully gathered in") strip the protagonists of agency ("won't have to think for themselves"), turning care into captivity. This deepens the protagonist's portrait: they are not just economically poor but politically infantilised. A wrong answer that treats the phrase as mere irony without connecting to loss of autonomy misses the analytical depth.

questions.q: Evaluate the speaker's final confession: "I can't help owning the great relief it would be / To put these people at one stroke out of their pain." Is this compassion or complicity? Justify with the poem's logic.
questions.a: It is compassion twisted by helplessness into complicity: the speaker's desire to "put them out of pain" mirrors the "good-doers'" fatal solutions, yet the closing rhetorical question ("how I should like you to come to me / And offer to put me gently out of my pain") implicates the reader, refusing easy resolution. A wrong answer that labels it purely "kind" or "cruel" ignores the poem's deliberate ambiguity and self-implication.

questions.q: Create a four-line stanza in free verse that gives voice to the protagonist's "childish longing" using imagery from the poem (berries, squash, mountain scene, city money). Do not copy lines.
questions.a:
We stack our quarts like prayers on splintered wood,  
Golden squash swells, waiting for a brake-light's glow —  
The mountain painted on our sign stays still,  
While city coins roll past, too bright to know.  
A poor answer would use generic sadness without the poem's specific symbols (quarts, squash, mountain sign, city money) or would copy Frost's phrasing.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: In poetry, the protagonist is the central figure or collective persona whose ______, struggles, and perspective drive the poem's emotional core and thematic development; unlike prose, a poetic protagonist may be a group (e.g., the rural poor) or the speaker's own persona, revealed through imagery, tone, and direct address rather than narrative action.

questions.a: In poetry, the protagonist is the central figure or collective persona whose experiences, struggles, and perspective drive the poem's emotional core and thematic development; unlike prose, a poetic protagonist may be a group (e.g., the rural poor) or the speaker's own persona, revealed through imagery, tone, and direct address rather.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about In poetry, the protagonist?
questions.a: Students often think the *poet* (Robert Frost) is the protagonist because he says "I" in the last stanza.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can identify the protagonist in "A Roadside Stand" (the rural stand-owners as a collective), cite at least three specific textual details (images, diction, contrasts) that reveal their economic condition, psychological state, and dignity, and explain how the poet's speaker positions himself in relation to them to deepen the.
